final_answer:
Let \(\chi\) be a quartic character of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), and let
\[
e=\chi(-1)=(-1)^{(p-1)/4}.
\]
Thus \(e=1\) if \(p\equiv1\pmod8\), and \(e=-1\) if \(p\equiv5\pmod8\).

The exact point count is
\[
\boxed{
\#C(\mathbb F_p)=
\begin{cases}
p+1, & p\equiv3\pmod4,\\[2mm]
p+1-6a, & p\equiv1\pmod8,\\[2mm]
p+1+2a, & p\equiv5\pmod8,
\end{cases}}
\]
where, in the last two cases, \(p=a^2+b^2\) and \(a\equiv1\pmod4\).

Sketch of derivation: for \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), fourth powers equal squares among nonzero elements, so the affine count reduces to
\[
\sum_{u+v=1}(1+\phi(u))(1+\phi(v))
=p+J(\phi,\phi)=p+1,
\]
and there are no points at infinity since \(-1\) is nonsquare.

For \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), expanding the number of fourth roots using \(1+\chi+\chi^2+\chi^3\) gives
\[
\#C(\mathbb F_p)=p+S+I,
\]
where \(I=4\) if \(p\equiv1\pmod8\) and \(I=0\) if \(p\equiv5\pmod8\). The nontrivial Jacobi-sum part is
\[
S=(1+2e)\bigl(J(\chi,\chi)+\overline{J(\chi,\chi)}\bigr)-2e-1.
\]
The classical quartic Jacobi sum evaluation gives
\[
J(\chi,\chi)+\overline{J(\chi,\chi)}=-2a,
\]
with \(a\equiv1\pmod4\) from \(p=a^2+b^2\). Hence
\[
\#C(\mathbb F_p)=p+1-2a(1+2e),
\]
which is exactly the two stated cases.
